items.prompt: Which type of NoSQL database is built around the simplest data model, where each record is looked up only by its unique identifier and the database treats the stored content as opaque?

options.label: Key-value store
Document database
Graph database
Wide-column store

rubric: A key-value store maps each unique key directly to a value.
Graph, wide-column and document stores organise data by relationships, column families or structured documents.

items.prompt: MongoDB stores each record in which format?

options.label: A key paired with a single string value
A node joined to others by edges
A row in a fixed-schema table
A JSON-like document (BSON)

rubric: MongoDB stores records as BSON, a binary JSON-like document.
Rows, nodes and plain keys describe relational, graph and key-value stores.

items.prompt: Which of these is a well-known graph database?

options.label: Cassandra
MongoDB
Redis
Neo4j

rubric: Neo4j is a graph database.
Redis is key-value, Cassandra is wide-column, MongoDB is document.

items.prompt: What does the term 'schema-less' (or flexible schema) mean for a document database?

options.label: Data is held only in memory and not saved to disk
Documents in one collection can have different fields
Documents are kept flat, so nested data is not supported
Each query must name a table definition before it runs

rubric: Flexible schema lets documents in a collection differ in fields.
Distractors confuse flexibility with no structure or no storage.

items.prompt: Which database is best known as an in-memory key-value store?

options.label: PostgreSQL
Redis
Cassandra
Neo4j

rubric: Redis is an in-memory key-value store.
Cassandra is wide-column; Neo4j is graph; PostgreSQL is relational.

items.prompt: Which of the following are NoSQL database categories? Select all that apply.

options.label: Graph
Document
Relational
Key-value

rubric: Document, graph and wide-column are NoSQL categories.
Relational databases are the SQL model, not a NoSQL category.

items.prompt: A new developer is reading about databases. The docs say, 'Apache Cassandra is designed to spread data across many servers with no single point of failure.' The developer wants to know which NoSQL category Cassandra belongs to. Which is it?

options.label: Key-value cache only
Graph database
Wide-column store
Document database

rubric: Cassandra is a wide-column store.
Learners often confuse it with document or graph stores because it is distributed.

items.prompt: Why do many NoSQL databases scale by adding more servers (horizontal scaling)?

options.label: Every server keeps a full copy of all the data and joins
They limit each server to one connected user at a time
Data is partitioned across machines, spreading the load
They keep all data on one very large central machine

rubric: Partitioning data across nodes lets load spread horizontally.
Distractors describe single-machine or incorrect designs.

items.prompt: What does 'eventual consistency' mean?

options.label: Every read returns the newest write, because writes wait for all replicas first
Writes are rejected until all replicas have agreed on a single value
Replicas may briefly differ but converge if no new writes occur
Data is kept only temporarily and is deleted once a set time passes

rubric: Eventual consistency means replicas converge over time.
Immediate agreement describes strong consistency instead.

items.prompt: A product document contains a nested list of customer reviews inside it. What is this modelling choice called?

options.label: Sharding the reviews
Embedding related data
Normalising into tables
Indexing the reviews

rubric: Placing related data inside a document is embedding.
Sharding, indexing and normalising are different concepts.

items.prompt: Which data fits a graph database most naturally?

options.label: Friend links between users in a social network
A cache of user session tokens looked up by session ID
Daily server logs appended in time order, one row per event
A list of invoices with the same fixed columns in every row

rubric: Graphs excel at highly connected data such as social links.
Sessions suit key-value, logs suit wide-column, fixed invoices suit relational.

items.prompt: What does this MongoDB query do? `db.users.find({ age: 30 })`

options.label: Returns users whose age equals 30
Deletes users aged 30
Adds a user aged 30
Counts every user in the database

rubric: find with a filter returns matching documents.
Other options confuse find with delete, insert or count.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe why a team might choose a NoSQL database over a relational one? Select all that apply.

options.label: The data shape varies between records
The app needs very fast lookups by a single key
They need to spread data across many servers
Every query requires complex multi-table joins

rubric: Flexible shape, horizontal scale and fast key lookups favour NoSQL.
Join-heavy workloads usually favour relational databases.

items.prompt: A shop stores shopping carts that are always read and written by user ID, and carts must load in milliseconds. Each cart is just a blob of items for one user. Which store type fits this need best?

options.label: Key-value store keyed by user ID
Wide-column store with no row keys
Relational database with many joined tables
Graph database with edges between carts

rubric: Access by a single key with simple values suits a key-value store.
Join-heavy or graph designs add unneeded complexity for this pattern.

items.prompt: Which type of NoSQL store is the most natural fit for a cache that maps a session token to that user's session data?

options.label: Graph database
Wide-column store
Key-value store
Document database with joins

rubric: A key-value store maps a unique key straight to a value, which is exactly a token-to-session lookup.
Graph and wide-column stores target relationship traversal and large partitioned tables, not simple lookups.

items.prompt: In a document database such as MongoDB, what is a document?

options.label: A fixed-width row that must match the column layout of every other row in its table
A text file that stores only the index for a collection
A self-contained JSON-like record whose fields can differ from its neighbours
A single key mapped to an opaque binary value that the database cannot look inside

rubric: A document is a self-describing record with named fields, and documents in one collection need not share a shape.
Distractors confuse documents with relational rows or with plain key-value blobs.

items.prompt: A database is configured to favour consistency over availability (CP). A network partition splits its nodes. What is the expected behaviour?

options.label: Every node keeps accepting writes and merges them later
Both sides keep serving reads and writes, then reconcile conflicts
Some requests are rejected or time out so data stays consistent
All nodes keep answering reads with whatever data they hold

rubric: A CP system sacrifices availability during a partition, so some requests fail rather than return inconsistent data.
Accepting writes everywhere and answering from local data describes an AP choice.

items.prompt: What does eventual consistency mean for a replicated NoSQL store?

options.label: If writes stop, replicas converge, but reads may briefly be stale
Replicas stay independent copies, so differing values are expected to persist
Reads return the latest write because a quorum must confirm each update first
Writes are held in a queue and applied to replicas in nightly batch jobs

rubric: Eventual consistency guarantees convergence after updates stop, while allowing temporary stale reads.
Distractors describe strong consistency, batch processing or no agreement at all.

items.prompt: Why is a graph database often chosen for a 'friends of friends' recommendation feature?

options.label: It guarantees eventual consistency across all of its replicas
It stores relationships as links that can be traversed directly
It keeps each user and their friends together in one JSON document
It precomputes the friend lists for users when data is first loaded

rubric: Graph databases store relationships as first-class links, so multi-hop traversals are cheap compared with repeated joins.
Other options describe document storage or consistency, which are not why graphs suit this task.

items.prompt: Which of the following are typical reasons to choose a NoSQL database over a relational one? Select all that apply.

options.label: Records have varying fields and the schema changes often
Every update must be atomic across several related tables
Data must scale horizontally across many commodity servers
Reports need many ad hoc joins across a dozen tables

rubric: Horizontal scaling and flexible schemas are classic NoSQL strengths.
Heavy ad hoc joins and multi-table atomic updates are where relational databases usually fit better.

items.prompt: An online shop sells books, which have an ISBN and page count, and shirts, which have a size and colour. The team is told a document database suits this catalogue. Why does it fit?

options.label: Documents are stored as opaque key-value blobs, so field-level queries need a scan
Document databases guarantee strongly consistent joins across collections by default
Document databases require one fixed set of columns declared up front for each collection
Each product document can hold its own fields, so no schema migration is needed

rubric: Documents in a collection can have different fields, which suits products with different attributes.
Distractors describe rigid relational schemas, guaranteed joins, or plain key-value limits.

items.prompt: A MongoDB collection `users` has documents with an `age` field. Which query returns users aged 30 or older?

options.label: `db.users.find({ age: { $gt: 30 } })`
`db.users.find({ $gte: { age: 30 } })`
`db.users.find({ age: { $gte: 30 } })`
`db.users.find({ age: >= 30 })`

rubric: `$gte` inside the field's condition object means greater than or equal to.
`$gt` excludes 30, and the other options use invalid syntax.

items.prompt: In Redis, these commands run in order: `SET counter 5`, `INCR counter`, `INCR counter`, `GET counter`. What does the last command return?
rubric: INCR adds 1 each time, so 5 becomes 6 then 7.
Returning 6 forgets one INCR; 55 treats the value as string concatenation.

items.prompt: In Redis you run `SET token:9 "abc" EX 60`. Ninety seconds later you run `GET token:9`. What is returned?

options.label: An error saying the key's time limit has passed
`"abc"`, because EX only affects writes
`nil`, because the key expired after 60 seconds
`"abc"`, but with its expiry time reset to 60

rubric: EX sets a 60-second time to live, after which the key is removed and GET returns nil.
Distractors assume the key persists or that expiry raises an error.

items.prompt: A blog app always shows a post with its few comments on one page. Comments are never queried on their own. How should you model this in MongoDB?

options.label: Store each comment in a separate collection and join on every read
Store all posts in one document and all comments in another
Keep comments in a graph and posts in a key-value store
Embed the comments as an array inside each post document

rubric: Data read together and bounded in size is best embedded, giving one read per page.
Separate collections or mixed stores add work without any benefit for this access pattern.

items.prompt: In Cassandra you must fetch the latest 20 events for one user quickly. Which table design fits this query?

options.label: Partition key `event_id`, no clustering column
Partition key `user_id`, clustering column `event_id` ascending
Partition key `timestamp`, clustering column `user_id`
Partition key `user_id`, clustering by `timestamp` DESC

rubric: Partitioning by user keeps one user's events together, and clustering by time descending returns the newest first.
Other designs spread a user's events across partitions or force scans.

items.prompt: A MongoDB collection holds three documents: `{name:"A", qty:5}`, `{name:"B", qty:12}`, `{name:"C", qty:20}`. Which filters return document B (possibly with others)? Select all that apply.

options.label: `{ name: "A" }`

rubric: qty 12 is above 10, below 15 and equal to 12, so those three filters match B.
`$gte: 20` matches only C, and name A matches only A.

items.prompt: A MongoDB collection `items` has the document `{ sku: "X1", stock: 10 }`. A customer buys 2 units of X1. You need to reduce the stored stock by 2 and leave other items untouched. Which command does this?

options.label: `db.items.updateOne({ sku: "X1" }, { $set: { stock: -2 } })`
`db.items.insertOne({ sku: "X1", stock: -2 })`
`db.items.updateOne({ sku: "X1" }, { $inc: { stock: -2 } })`
`db.items.updateMany({}, { $inc: { stock: -2 } })`

rubric: `updateOne` with a sku filter and `$inc` of -2 lowers only X1's stock to 8.
`$set` overwrites with -2, an empty filter changes every item, and insert adds a duplicate.

items.prompt: In Redis you run `SET session:42 abc EX 60`, wait 30 seconds, then run `SET session:42 def`. What does `TTL session:42` return immediately afterwards?
rubric: A plain SET overwrites the value and clears any existing expiry, so the key now has no TTL (-1).
Distractors assume the old TTL is kept (30) or reset (60); -2 means the key does not exist.

items.prompt: A MongoDB `orders` collection holds: A (status shipped, total 100), B (shipped, 150), C (pending, 300), D (shipped, 200). Which documents does `db.orders.find({status:"shipped", total:{$gte:100}}).sort({total:1})` return, in order?

options.label: A, B, C, D
D, B, A
A, B, D
B, D

rubric: $gte includes A at exactly 100, the status filter drops C, and sort 1 is ascending: A, B, D.
Distractors reverse the sort direction, treat $gte as $gt, or ignore the status filter.

items.prompt: A Cassandra table is defined with `PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), posted_at) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (posted_at DESC)`. Which query fetches a user's 10 newest posts without `ALLOW FILTERING`?

options.label: `SELECT * FROM posts WHERE user_id > 7 LIMIT 10`
`SELECT * FROM posts ORDER BY posted_at DESC LIMIT 10`
`SELECT * FROM posts WHERE posted_at > '2024-01-01' LIMIT 10`
`SELECT * FROM posts WHERE user_id = 7 LIMIT 10`

rubric: Restricting the partition key by equality reads one partition already sorted newest first, so LIMIT 10 gives the latest posts.
Distractors skip the partition key, use a range on it, or order across partitions, none of which Cassandra serves efficiently.

items.prompt: In MongoDB, a user profile always displays at most 3 saved addresses, and addresses are never queried on their own. How should you model them?

options.label: Serialise them into one string field on the user, since arrays cannot be stored in documents
Put them in a separate addresses collection and join them in an application loop on each read
Store each address as an unlinked top-level document, since document stores need flat records
Embed them as an array in the user document, since they are bounded and always read together

rubric: Small, bounded data that is always read with its parent belongs embedded, giving one read and atomic updates.
Distractors apply relational normalisation habits or wrongly claim documents cannot hold arrays.

items.prompt: Redis sorted set `leaderboard` stores player names scored by points. Which command returns the 3 players with the highest points, best first, with their scores?

options.label: `ZRANGE leaderboard 0 2 WITHSCORES`
`LRANGE leaderboard 0 2`
`ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 2 WITHSCORES`
`HGETALL leaderboard`

rubric: ZREVRANGE orders by descending score, so indexes 0 to 2 are the top 3.
ZRANGE returns the lowest scores first; LRANGE and HGETALL apply to lists and hashes, not sorted sets.

items.prompt: A Cassandra table has `PRIMARY KEY ((country), city, user_id)`. Which queries can be served without `ALLOW FILTERING`? Select all that apply.

options.label: `WHERE country = 'DE' AND city = 'Bonn'`
`WHERE country = 'DE'`
`WHERE user_id = 5`
`WHERE country = 'DE' AND city = 'Bonn' AND user_id = 5`
`WHERE city = 'Bonn'`

rubric: Queries must restrict the partition key and then clustering columns in order, so the first three work.
Filtering on city or user_id alone skips the partition key and would need a full scan.

items.prompt: An online shop stores each cart as one MongoDB document: `{_id: 1, items: [{sku: "A1", quantity: 2}, {sku: "B7", quantity: 1}]}`. A customer clicks '+' on item A1. You must raise its quantity by one atomically, without reading the cart first. Which update does this?

options.label: `updateOne({_id:1, "items.sku":"A1"}, {$inc:{"items.$.quantity":1}})`
`updateOne({_id:1}, {$push:{items:{sku:"A1", quantity:1}}})`
`updateOne({_id:1, "items.sku":"A1"}, {$set:{"items.$.quantity":3}})`
`updateOne({_id:1}, {$inc:{quantity:1}})`

rubric: Matching the array element in the filter and using the positional $ with $inc increments only that element atomically.
$set with a hardcoded 3 needs a prior read and can lose updates; $push adds a duplicate entry; the last option touches a nonexistent top-level field.

items.prompt: `explain()` for `db.events.find({userId: 5}).sort({createdAt: -1}).limit(20)` shows an IXSCAN on a single-field `userId` index followed by an in-memory SORT stage. Latency grows as users accumulate events. What is the cause?

options.label: The userId index is not being used, so the query falls back to a full collection scan of every event
Sorting only benefits from an index once the collection is sharded, so the single-node index cannot help
The limit is applied before the filter and sort, so the server loads far too many documents first
The index cannot supply createdAt order, so all of the user's matches are fetched, then sorted

rubric: Only a compound index such as {userId:1, createdAt:-1} returns matches already ordered, so the current plan sorts every match for the user.
The IXSCAN shows the index is used; limit applies after sorting; sharding is not required for sort.

items.prompt: A Cassandra table uses partition key `sensor_id` and clustering key `ts`. One sensor writes 1000 readings per second. After months, reads and compactions for that sensor are slow while other sensors are fine. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Cassandra cannot hold time series, so data was silently dropped
The sensor's partition grows without bound, so it becomes huge and hot
Replication factor is too low, so the other nodes cannot serve the reads
The clustering key ts forces every read to scan all other sensors' partitions

rubric: Using only sensor_id as the partition key makes one partition grow forever; adding a time bucket to the key bounds it.
Other sensors being fine rules out cluster-wide causes like replication factor; clustering does not scan other partitions.

items.prompt: A user posts a comment; the app writes it to a MongoDB primary, then reloads the page reading with `readPreference: secondary`. Sometimes the new comment is missing, but it appears seconds later. What explains this?

options.label: Documents become visible only after the oplog is truncated on the primary
The secondary may not have replicated the write yet, so the read returned older data
The comment collection is missing an index, so new documents are hidden until it rebuilds
The write was rejected by the primary and was retried later by the driver

rubric: Reads from a lagging secondary can miss recent writes; reading from the primary or using causal consistency fixes it.
The write succeeded, indexes do not hide documents, and oplog truncation is unrelated to visibility.

items.prompt: A site caches a popular product page in Redis with a 5-minute TTL. Every 5 minutes the database spikes to near overload for a few seconds, then recovers. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Many concurrent requests miss the just-expired key and all rebuild it from the database
Each expiry makes Redis rewrite its whole dataset to disk, stalling reads that then fall through to the database
The database leaks connections whenever Redis returns a cached value, until the pool is exhausted every 5 minutes
Redis evicts the key early because the TTL is longer than memory allows, so reads fall back to the database

rubric: A cache stampede happens when a hot key expires and many requests recompute it at once; locking or jittered TTLs mitigate it.
The periodic pattern matches the TTL, not eviction, connection leaks on hits, or persistence rewrites.

items.prompt: A 'friends up to 4 hops away' query runs in seconds on a relational `friendships(a, b)` table with indexes but in milliseconds on a graph database. Which analysis explains the gap?

options.label: The graph store avoids revisiting friends already reached through a cycle, and the relational engine has to re-expand them at every hop
The graph store keeps the working set in memory, while the relational engine pays disk reads for each index lookup on every hop
Each hop adds a self-join whose intermediate rows multiply, while the graph store follows stored links from one start node
The relational index on a two-column table helps little here, since each hop joins on a non-selective key and scans most of the table

rubric: Relational cost grows with joined intermediate results across hops; graph traversal touches only the neighbourhood reachable from the start node.
Distractors claim false limits (no indexes, memory only, cycle handling) instead of the join versus traversal cost difference.

items.prompt: A blog stores each post as one MongoDB document with all comments embedded in an array. Popular posts reach 200,000 comments. Which problems follow from this design? Select all that apply.

options.label: Each read of the post loads every comment even when a page shows only 20
The document can approach the maximum document size limit and writes will fail
The collection can no longer be sharded across servers
Comments can no longer be filtered by any field inside the array

rubric: Unbounded embedding hits the document size cap and forces large reads; referencing comments in their own collection avoids both.
Array fields remain queryable and indexable, and sharding depends on the shard key, not on document size.

items.prompt: A Dynamo-style store has replication factor N=3 and the client uses read quorum R=1 and write quorum W=1. Users sometimes read stale values right after writing. The team wants every successful read to see the latest successful write, at minimal extra latency. Which setting achieves this?

options.label: R=2, W=2, because the read and write quorums must overlap in at least one replica
R=2, W=1, because reading from more replicas guarantees seeing every write
R=1, W=2, because writing to more replicas makes any single replica current
R=1, W=1 with read repair, because repair fixes stale replicas before each read

rubric: Guaranteed overlap needs R + W > N; 2 + 2 = 4 > 3, so every read quorum includes a replica with the latest write.
R=2,W=1 and R=1,W=2 sum to 3, which can miss; read repair fixes replicas after the read, not before.

items.prompt: A Cassandra table `orders_by_user` has partition key `user_id`. A new query `SELECT * FROM orders_by_user WHERE status = 'pending'` is rejected or, with filtering forced, runs very slowly. What is the root cause?

options.label: The status column is a string, and string comparisons cannot be pushed down to the storage engine
The clustering order of the table forces results to be sorted before the filter is applied
The query filters on a non-key column, so every partition on every node would have to be scanned
The table's replication factor is too low to serve filtered reads from more than one node

rubric: The table was modelled for lookups by user_id; filtering on an unkeyed column means a full cluster scan.
Distractors blame data type, replication or sorting, none of which explain the cost.

items.prompt: In MongoDB, each `product` document embeds an array of every review. Over months, update latency for popular products rises steadily, while unpopular ones stay fast. Which diagnosis best fits?

options.label: The unbounded embedded array makes popular documents large, so each update rewrites and loads more data
Popular products are being routed to a single replica, which leaves secondaries idle during writes
The default index on `_id` degrades as the collection grows past a certain number of documents
Reviews should be stored as strings rather than sub-documents, since sub-documents are slower to parse

rubric: Unbounded embedding grows documents for hot items, raising I/O per update and nearing size limits.
The _id index and replica routing would affect all products equally, not just popular ones.

items.prompt: A Redis Cluster holds millions of keys spread evenly across shards by hash slot. One shard sits at 95% CPU while others idle at 10%. Traffic analysis shows most requests hit `counter:homepage`. What explains the imbalance?

options.label: The shard is running out of memory, which makes Redis fall back to disk and burn CPU on swapping
A single hot key maps to one slot on one shard, so even key distribution does not spread its load
Hash slots were assigned unevenly, so that shard holds far more keys than the others
Redis Cluster replicates every key to all shards, so the busiest shard does extra synchronisation work

rubric: Load is determined by access pattern; one key lives on exactly one primary regardless of even key counts.
Uneven slot assignment contradicts the stated even key spread.

items.prompt: A Cassandra keyspace uses replication factor 3. An app writes at consistency `ONE` and reads at consistency `ONE`. Users sometimes read stale data right after writing. Which analysis is correct?

options.label: Write and read replica counts sum to 2, which does not exceed 3, so a read can miss the written replica
Read repair is disabled by default, so replicas can never converge without a manual repair
Cassandra only replicates asynchronously after 24 hours, so any read inside that window is stale
Timestamps are assigned by the reader, so concurrent reads pick whichever replica answers last

rubric: Strong consistency needs R + W > RF; 1 + 1 is not greater than 3, so the sets may not overlap.
Other options invent replication delays or timestamp behaviour that does not exist.

items.prompt: A MongoDB collection of events is sharded on `createdAt` (ascending timestamp) with range-based sharding. Insert throughput is far below what the cluster's total capacity suggests. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: All new inserts fall in the highest chunk range, so one shard takes the whole write load
Range-based sharding cannot be combined with secondary indexes, which slows every write
Timestamps are too large to hash, so the balancer repeatedly migrates chunks between shards
Each shard must acknowledge every insert, so adding shards linearly adds write latency

rubric: A monotonically increasing shard key directs all inserts to the chunk at the top end, creating a hot shard.
The other options misstate how shards acknowledge writes or index support.

items.prompt: A team implements a job queue in Cassandra: one partition per queue, rows inserted and then deleted after processing. Reads of 'next pending job' get slower over days. Which factors contribute? Select all that apply.

options.label: The queue's single partition concentrates all reads and deletes on the same replicas
The read repeatedly scans from the start of the partition across deleted entries
Cassandra's clustering columns are stored unsorted, so each read re-sorts the partition
Deleted rows leave tombstones that reads must scan past until compaction removes them

rubric: Queue patterns accumulate tombstones in a hot partition, and reads from the head must skip them.
Clustering columns are stored sorted on disk, so re-sorting is not a cause.

items.prompt: A team moved a relational reporting model into MongoDB, keeping separate `customers`, `orders` and `order_items` collections. The dashboard now uses `$lookup` across all three and takes 20 seconds; the same dashboard was fast in SQL. Reads are about 95% of traffic and are always 'order with its items and customer name'. What best explains the slowdown?

options.label: The orders collection has too few indexed fields, so the planner scans it fully and no index can speed up the lookups
MongoDB has weaker join support than SQL, so `$lookup` copies each joined collection into memory before matching rows
The model was not reshaped around the read pattern, so joins run at query time
Sharding is usually enabled by default, so aggregations are forced to run on a single node and cannot use other servers

rubric: A normalised model imported unchanged ignores that document stores favour embedding data read together.
Other options misdescribe $lookup or sharding and do not follow from the stated facts.

items.prompt: Criteria: sub-millisecond reads, data is disposable after 30 minutes, no queries beyond lookup by session id, and loss of a session is acceptable. Which store is the best fit for web session data?

options.label: A document database with a compound index on user and creation time
A graph database, since sessions relate users to devices and pages
A wide-column store with per-session partitions and tunable quorum reads
An in-memory key-value store with per-key expiry set to 30 minutes

rubric: Lookup by id, TTL expiry, low latency and tolerable loss match an in-memory key-value store.
Other options add query or durability features the criteria do not need.

items.prompt: A shopping cart service must stay writable during network partitions, tolerate temporary divergence, and never lose an added item. Which design best meets these criteria?

options.label: A leaderless replicated store that accepts writes anywhere and merges carts on read
A store that locks the cart row across regions until every replica acknowledges each change
A cache-only design with a short TTL so stale carts expire before they can conflict
A single-primary store that rejects writes on the minority side to guarantee linearizability

rubric: Availability under partition with no lost items points to an AP design with merge, as in Dynamo-style carts.
Rejecting or locking writes sacrifices availability; a TTL cache can lose items.

items.prompt: In MongoDB, a blog post has on average 8 comments, rarely more than 40, and comments are always displayed with the post and never queried alone. Criteria: minimal read round trips and simple writes. Which model is best?

options.label: Duplicate the post's fields into every comment document so a read never needs a second document
Keep comments in a graph collection so replies can be traversed with `$graphLookup`
Embed comments in the post document, since the set is small, bounded and read together
Store comments in a separate collection keyed by post id, so post documents stay small and comments can be indexed alone

rubric: Small, bounded, always co-read children favour embedding for one read and atomic writes.
Referencing adds round trips, and copying posts or graph models solve problems not stated.

items.prompt: A proposal puts Cassandra behind a BI tool so analysts can run ad hoc queries with joins and arbitrary filters on any column. Judged against those criteria, what is the strongest critique?

options.label: Cassandra's storage engine caps tables at a size too small for the data volumes analysts normally query
Cassandra only offers a procedural query language, which BI tools cannot generate or send to the database
Tables are modelled per query, so ad hoc filters and joins fit poorly without a separate analytic store
Cassandra's eventual consistency means analysts can only read data that is a full day behind the writes

rubric: Query-first modelling and lack of joins make arbitrary analysis a poor fit; export to an analytic system instead.
Cassandra scales to large data volumes and does not impose a day-long delay or procedural-only language.

items.prompt: Redis is proposed as the sole store for order records. Config: RDB snapshot every 5 minutes, no replicas. Requirement: lose at most about one second of orders after a crash. Which change best meets it at modest cost?

options.label: Enable AOF with fsync every second, and add a replica for failover
Shorten the RDB snapshot interval to 60 seconds and keep one node
Raise the memory limit so snapshots finish before the next one starts
Set eviction policy to allkeys-lru so older orders are dropped first, then add a replica

rubric: AOF with everysec bounds loss to about one second, and a replica improves recovery.
A 60-second snapshot still risks a minute of loss; memory limits and eviction do not bound crash loss.

items.prompt: Criteria: a financial ledger needs atomic multi-record transfers, enforced constraints, and flexible audit queries across accounts. Which arguments validly favour a relational database over a typical NoSQL store here? Select all that apply.

options.label: Multi-row ACID transactions and foreign keys are mature defaults, protecting transfer invariants
The schema is enforced by the database, reducing the risk of malformed ledger entries
Ad hoc joins and aggregates across accounts are first-class, which suits audit queries
Normalised tables let each account's writes be sharded across nodes more simply, which helps ledger throughput

rubric: Transactions, joins and enforced schema match the stated ledger criteria.
The claim of universally better horizontal write scaling is false; it is often the reverse.

items.prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS on a sharded document database has 2,000 tenants; the largest holds 40% of all data. Almost every query filters by tenant and by record id. The team must balance writes evenly and keep tenant queries on few shards. Which shard key is best?

options.label: A compound key of `tenantId` and a hashed `recordId`, splitting the big tenant while keeping tenant routing
`createdAt` ascending, which spreads reads over time but sends every new write to the one newest shard
`tenantId` alone, which keeps each tenant's data together but leaves the 40% tenant stuck on a single shard
A random UUID per write, which spreads load evenly but turns every tenant query into a scatter-gather

rubric: The compound key keeps tenant-targeted routing and splits the large tenant across shards.
The other keys fail one stated criterion: even writes or targeted queries.

items.prompt: A Cassandra keyspace uses replication factor 3 in one datacenter. Requirement: a read must see the latest acknowledged write, and both reads and writes must keep working with one replica down. Which consistency pairing best meets this?

options.label: Write ANY and read ALL, since every read then contacts every replica holding data
Write QUORUM and read QUORUM, since 2 + 2 > 3 and each needs only 2 replicas
Write ONE and read QUORUM, since a single write and a quorum read always overlap
Write ONE and read ONE, since replication copies data fast enough to be current

rubric: Quorum on both sides gives R + W > N while tolerating one down replica.
Write ONE plus read QUORUM gives 1 + 2 = 3, which does not exceed N, and read ALL fails when a replica is down.

items.prompt: An orders collection takes 50k inserts/s. Most queries filter by customerId, and a few customers each generate about 20% of the traffic. Which MongoDB shard key best balances even writes with targeted queries?

options.label: Hashed customerId, which spreads customers evenly across shards and keeps each customer's queries targeted
Ascending orderId, which keeps new inserts together so index writes stay fast on a single shard
Compound {customerId: 1, _id: 1}, which targets queries and can split a big customer
createdAt timestamp, which makes recent-order queries land on a single shard each time

rubric: Adding _id to customerId gives high cardinality, so heavy customers can be split while queries stay targeted.
Hashed customerId keeps one customer in one chunk, which becomes a jumbo hotspot, and monotonic keys concentrate inserts on one shard.

items.prompt: Redis is the system of record for user sessions. Requirement: after a crash, lose at most about one second of writes, with minimal impact on write latency. Which persistence setup is the best judgement?

options.label: RDB snapshots every 5 minutes, since snapshots are compact and fast to reload on restart
An async replica with no disk persistence, since the replica holds a copy of every write
AOF with appendfsync everysec, which bounds loss near one second at modest latency cost
AOF with appendfsync always, since fsync on each write gives the strongest durability guarantee

rubric: AOF everysec matches the one-second loss bound without an fsync on every write.
Fsync always adds notable latency, and RDB or async replication can lose much more than a second.

items.prompt: A Cassandra table has PRIMARY KEY (sensor_id, ts). Each sensor writes 1,000 readings/s and queries read the last hour per sensor. After months, reads slow down and compaction struggles. Which critique is most valid?

options.label: A secondary index on ts is needed so hour-range queries stop scanning the whole partition
Each sensor's partition grows without bound; add a time bucket like the day to the partition key
Clustering by ts is wrong; a random clustering order would spread the writes across nodes
The replication factor is too low; raising it will shrink each partition across the cluster

rubric: Unbounded wide partitions hurt reads and compaction; bucketing bounds them while keeping range reads.
Replication copies partitions rather than shrinking them, and a secondary index does not fix partition size.

items.prompt: Product documents have at most 15 variants (size, colour, stock). Variants are always displayed with the product, their stock is updated individually, and they are never queried on their own. Which MongoDB modelling is the best trade-off?

options.label: Reference variants in a separate collection, since splitting data always makes reads faster by keeping documents small
Make each variant a top-level product document, since duplicating the shared fields is harmless here
Embed variants as an array, since they are bounded, read together and updatable atomically with the parent
Reference variants in a separate collection, since arrays inside documents cannot be updated in place

rubric: Bounded, co-read, co-updated data is the classic case for embedding.
Positional updates on arrays work, and splitting adds extra lookups without benefit here.

items.prompt: A Dynamo-style store resolves concurrent writes to the same item with last-write-wins on timestamps. Which statements correctly judge this approach? Select all that apply.

options.label: It guarantees that no acknowledged write is ever lost, even under concurrency
Vector clocks remove any need for an application-level merge of siblings
A write from a node with a lagging clock can overwrite a causally later write
Concurrent updates to different fields of one item can be silently discarded

rubric: LWW depends on clock agreement and keeps only one whole version, so skew and concurrent edits cause lost data.
Vector clocks only detect concurrency; something must still merge the siblings.

items.prompt: A team runs Postgres with a friendships table (user_id, friend_id) indexed on both columns. They have 40k users averaging 80 friends, and need friends-of-friends suggestions in under 100 ms, a few times per second. A colleague proposes migrating to a graph database. What is the best judgement?

options.label: Migrate: graph engines always answer traversals faster, regardless of data size or hop depth
Keep Postgres: a two-hop indexed self-join touches roughly 6,400 rows and meets the target at this scale
Migrate: relational joins cannot traverse relationships, so any friends query needs a graph engine
Move friendships to a key-value store, since one lookup per user avoids joins entirely

rubric: At small scale and shallow depth, indexed joins are fast enough, so migration cost is not justified.
Graph advantages appear with deep or large traversals, and the claims that joins cannot traverse or that graphs are always faster are false.

items.prompt: Design a Cassandra table for chat. Requirement: fetch the newest 50 messages of a room, newest first; rooms may hold millions of messages; partitions must stay bounded; a normal read should hit one partition. Which design fits?

options.label: PRIMARY KEY (room_id, sent_at) with clustering order sent_at DESC, one partition per room
PRIMARY KEY ((sent_at), room_id), so that each partition holds one moment of all rooms
PRIMARY KEY (msg_id) with a secondary index on room_id, so each room's messages are found by the index
PRIMARY KEY ((room_id, day), sent_at, msg_id) with clustering order sent_at DESC

rubric: A day bucket bounds partition size, and DESC clustering returns the newest rows first from one partition.
A per-room partition is unbounded, and time-based or indexed designs scatter reads across many nodes.

items.prompt: Design Redis rate limiting: 100 requests per rolling 60 seconds per user, enforced consistently across 20 app servers, with no race between checking and recording a request. Which design meets every constraint?

options.label: A per-user counter using INCR and EXPIRE 60, which can let 200 requests through at a window boundary
Each server keeps its own in-memory counter and allows 5 requests per minute per user on each server
GET the count, compare it in application code, then SET the incremented count with a 60 second TTL
A per-user sorted set of timestamps; a Lua script trims old entries, counts and adds atomically

rubric: A sorted set gives a true rolling window, and a Lua script makes trim, count and add atomic across servers.
Fixed windows allow boundary bursts, per-server counters are not consistent, and read-then-write has a race.

items.prompt: Design DynamoDB keys for one table. Access patterns: (a) list a customer's orders newest first, (b) fetch a single order by orderId alone. Neither may use a scan. Which design satisfies both?

options.label: PK = CUSTOMER#id, SK = ORDER#timestamp#orderId, plus a GSI keyed on orderId
PK = CUSTOMER#id, SK = orderId, sorting client-side after reading, with no way to look up by orderId
PK = timestamp, SK = customerId, with a GSI on orderId to fetch single orders quickly
PK = orderId, SK = timestamp, and list a customer's orders with a filtered scan on customerId

rubric: The composite sort key gives ordered per-customer queries and the GSI serves lookup by orderId.
The other designs need a scan, give no ordering, or leave pattern (b) unserved.

items.prompt: A MongoDB document holding a like counter receives 5,000 increments/s and becomes a write hotspot. Design a fix that removes the hotspot and tolerates reads that are about a second stale. Which fix fits?

options.label: Move the counter to a larger replica set and send the increments to secondaries to share the load
Split into N counter documents, increment a random one, and sum them or cache the total on read
Read the counter, add one in application code, and write it back using majority write concern
Add an index on the counter field so that each increment locates the document much faster

rubric: Sharded counters spread writes across documents, and the sum is cheap and slightly stale.
Indexing does not reduce contention, read-modify-write races, and secondaries cannot accept writes.

items.prompt: Design a permission model: users belong to nested groups, documents sit in nested folders, and access inherits downward. Group membership changes hourly and revocation must take effect immediately. Which design fits?

options.label: A cache of every user-document answer kept 24 hours and refreshed by a nightly batch job
A graph with MEMBER_OF, CONTAINS and CAN_READ edges; check by path query, revoke by deleting one edge
A flattened array of permitted user ids on each document, rebuilt whenever group membership changes
Each user's group list copied into every document at write time to make checks a single lookup

rubric: Inherited access is a path-existence problem, and revoking one edge takes effect at once with no fan-out rewrite.
Flattened or cached copies go stale or require large rewrites after each membership change.

items.prompt: A hot product key is cached in Redis with a 5 second TTL. When it expires, 2,000 requests/s hit the database. Constraints: database load stays flat at expiry, a few seconds of staleness is acceptable, and many keys are bulk-loaded together. Which belong in the design? Select all that apply.

options.label: Shortening the TTL to 500 ms so each refresh covers less traffic
Removing the TTL and refreshing only after a restart
A single-flight lock so only one request recomputes an expired key
Serving the stale value while one background refresh runs
Random jitter on TTLs so bulk-loaded keys do not expire together

rubric: Single-flight and stale-while-revalidate stop the stampede on a hot key, and jitter spreads bulk expiry.
A shorter TTL increases refresh load, and no TTL breaks freshness.

items.prompt: A shopping cart service runs in two regions that both must keep accepting writes during a network partition, using a Dynamo-style store. In one region a user adds a book; in the other, a phone case. After healing, no added item may vanish, and removals should persist where possible. Which design fits?

options.label: Store the whole cart as one value and let last-write-wins by timestamp choose the surviving version
Route all cart writes to one region and reject writes in the other region during a partition
Model the cart as an add/remove set with per-item tags, merging replicas by union and tombstones
Require ALL-replica write consistency so that both regions agree before acknowledging each add

rubric: A set CRDT merges concurrent adds and removes without losing items and stays available in both regions.
LWW drops one side's item, and the single-region or ALL-write options give up availability during the partition.
